sentences.text: Centrosaurus grew to lengths of 5 to 5.5 meters and weighed between 2 and 2.5 metric tons.
This species is easily recognized by two large hornlets that curve forward over the back of its skull.
It also possessed a single nose horn that could curve either forward or backward depending on the individual.
The name Centrosaurus comes from Greek words meaning 'point' and 'lizard'.
This name refers to the row of small horns along the frill edge, not the nose horn which was unknown at the time.
In 2020, researchers described a rare and aggressive osteosarcoma cancer in an adult Centrosaurus fossil from Alberta.
One specimen discovered in 1989 suffered from a crippling cancer in its right fibula bone.
The first fossils were found by Lawrence Lambe in Alberta, Canada, near the Red Deer River.
Thousands of remains were later uncovered near Hilda, Alberta, forming what is believed to be the largest dinosaur bonebed ever found.
These massive bonebeds stretch for kilometers and contain thousands of specimens of various ages and health conditions.
Like other members of the Ceratopsidae family, its jaws were built to slice through tough vegetation.
Gigantic bone beds indicate that these animals lived in large groups and traveled together.
A 2009 study suggested that lesions on their skulls resulted from fighting with other Centrosaurus rather than attacks by predators.
The frills of this dinosaur were too thin to offer protection against predators, unlike the thicker frills of Triceratops.
Living in a herd likely allowed an individual with severe cancer to survive longer than expected.
Scientists note that the frills were not effective defensive structures against larger hunters.
The genus Centrosaurus provides the name for the subfamily Centrosaurinae.
Its closest relatives appear to be Styracosaurus and Monoclonius.
Centrosaurus is a member of the larger Ceratopsidae family.
Fossils date to the period between 76.5 and 75.5 million years ago.
Remains have only been found in southern Alberta, even though the region held many Judithian dinosaurs.
Despite being one of the most common Judithian dinosaurs, fossils are restricted to southern Alberta.
Large herbivorous ceratopsians in Late Cretaceous North America had surprisingly small geographic ranges despite their size and mobility.
Centrosaurus appears lower in the rock layers than Styracosaurus, suggesting it was pushed out as the environment changed.
There is ongoing debate over whether Centrosaurus and Monoclonius are valid genera or represent different sexes of the same species.
Peter Dodson argued in 1996 that Centrosaurus, Styracosaurus, and Monoclonius should be kept as separate genera.
Significant discussion continues regarding whether these names refer to distinct genera or sexual variations within a single species.
While sexual dimorphism has been proposed for the basal ceratopsian Protoceratops, no firm evidence supports this in any ceratopsian.
